title: Kalimantan railway: After Whoosh, Indonesia can’t afford another rush job
gist: Indonesia is again courting China (and Russia) to build a Kalimantan freight railway of up to 2,772 km - roughly US$40bn if scaled from an abandoned 203 km, US$3bn plan - and the author argues the Whoosh high-speed line's cost overruns and Jakarta's 60% KCIC bailout show risk sits with Indonesian borrowers, so Jakarta should stage corridors, lock in freight contracts first and spread risk to miners and plantations.

insights.claim: President Prabowo Subianto has ordered state railway operator Kereta Api Indonesia and the transport ministry to advance a Kalimantan railway, with planners studying a route up to 2,772 km linking ports, industrial areas and resource regions.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Large pipeline for rail contractors and resource logistics in Borneo.

insights.claim: Jakarta wants private investors rather than the state budget to fund the Kalimantan railway and has been talking to Chinese and Russian companies about building it.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: China vs Russia competition for a multi-billion rail contract; watch Chinese SOE contractors.

insights.claim: An earlier 203 km Kalimantan line to Balikpapan port, priced at about US$3 billion, was abandoned in 2022 after Russian Railways pulled out; scaling that cost to 2,772 km implies roughly US$40 billion (a rough illustration, not a forecast).
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Scale implies major fiscal/contingent-liability risk for Indonesia; Russian reliability as a partner is questionable.
insights.locator: An earlier plan shows a realistic starting size

insights.claim: Kalimantan holds large coal, palm oil, timber and mineral reserves but lacks Java's transport network; freight will fill wagons as long as commodity demand exists, unlike passenger traffic.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Rail would lower logistics costs for Kalimantan coal/palm oil/mining producers.
insights.locator: Kalimantan holds huge coal, palm oil

insights.claim: Nusantara, Indonesia's new capital, is taking shape in Kalimantan, adding to the stakes of getting the railway right.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Railway ties into the Nusantara capital build-out.

themes.theme: Whoosh lessons: risk sits with the borrower

insights.claim: The Jakarta-Bandung Whoosh line was financed about 75% by a China Development Bank loan to joint venture PT KCIC, majority-owned by Indonesian state firms; China acted as lender and builder, not a risk-absorbing investor.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Belt and Road rail deals leave credit risk with host-country SOEs, not Chinese banks.
insights.locator: But Whoosh was never a Chinese-funded gift

insights.claim: Whoosh cost about US$7.3 billion, well over budget, due to slow land acquisition, moved utility lines, rising construction costs and delayed financing.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Benchmark for Indonesian mega-project overrun risk.
insights.locator: Whoosh’s real lesson sits mostly with Indonesia

insights.claim: Indonesia's finance ministry will take a 60% stake in PT KCIC in 2026 to stabilise its debt, while Chinese lenders were repaid regardless.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Shows contingent liabilities of SOE infrastructure migrating to the sovereign balance sheet.
insights.quote: It is Indonesian borrowers, not Chinese banks, who have to worry whether a railway earns enough to service its debt
insights.locator: Whoosh’s real lesson sits mostly with Indonesia

insights.claim: Whoosh has carried more than 16 million passengers since opening in 2023 as Southeast Asia's first high-speed railway, cutting a three-hour trip to under an hour.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Operational usage is solid even though financing is strained.
insights.locator: Beijing’s main reference point is Whoosh

insights.claim: In 2015 China beat Japan's bid for Whoosh partly by offering to skip the government guarantee Tokyo wanted, a concession that later left more risk with Indonesia.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Headline-friendly Chinese terms can hide risk transfer; compare bid structures, not just price.
insights.locator: Beijing has faced a contest like this before

insights.claim: Chinese state-linked lenders provided about US$70 billion to Indonesia in 2000-2023, over 90% as loans, per AidData, a fraction of Indonesia's total infrastructure spending.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Chinese finance in Indonesia is loan-based and smaller than perceived.
insights.locator: That role is also smaller in scale

insights.claim: Jakarta should stage the Kalimantan railway, starting with corridors where freight demand is already strong, and lock in long-term freight agreements before construction to give lenders real security.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Offtake-backed staging would make the project more bankable for lenders.
insights.locator: Given numbers that size, Jakarta should stage

insights.claim: If a bank lends to the project, KAI guarantees the loan and an Indonesian state fund guarantees KAI, the ultimate risk still sits with Jakarta regardless of paperwork.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Layered SOE guarantees are quasi-sovereign debt; factor into Indonesian fiscal risk.
insights.locator: The financing structure deserves as much scrutiny

insights.claim: Spreading railway risk across Indonesian banks, state firms and the mining and plantation companies that benefit directly would leave Indonesia less exposed than with Whoosh.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Kalimantan miners/plantation firms may be asked to co-fund or commit offtake.
insights.locator: The financing structure deserves as much scrutiny

insights.claim: With Russia rather than Japan as China's rival for the Kalimantan railway, Jakarta should use the competition to negotiate the best terms.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: Bid competition may improve terms; watch contract award.
insights.locator: This time Russia, not Japan, is the rival

insights.claim: The Makassar-Parepare railway in South Sulawesi, built via a public-private partnership pairing a Chinese construction firm with Indonesian companies that handled operations while localising staff, is a workable model.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: PPP model is the likely template for future Chinese-Indonesian rail projects.

insights.claim: The right sequence is cargo commitments first, binding contracts second, financing third, construction last; getting it wrong means Indonesia pays.
insights.speaker: Muhammad Zulfikar Rakhmat
insights.so_what: A checklist to track Kalimantan project progress and credit quality.
insights.quote: cargo commitments first, binding contracts second, financing third, construction last
